summary: Specifies the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, based on the One-way Active Measurement Protocol, for measuring round-trip or two-way network metrics between two devices. OWAMP could be used both ways for one-way metrics but could not handle round trips. TWAMP is standards-track and has been extended later.

eli5.summary: To find how long a ball takes to go to a friend and back, you throw it and time it. TWAMP does that with test packets over a network.

questions: how to measure round trip delay between network devices
subtitle: Measure round-trip network performance by bouncing test packets off a reflector, using the same architecture as OWAMP.

tldr.problem: OWAMP (RFC 4656) measures one-way metrics but cannot do round-trip or two-way measurements, and the common alternative, ICMP Echo (ping), has documented issues.
tldr.mechanism: TWAMP reuses OWAMP's control and test design. A control connection on TCP port 862 sets up sessions, then a Session-Sender sends UDP test packets and a Session-Reflector timestamps each one and sends it straight back.
tldr.outcome: Round-trip measurements need no clock synchronization between the two ends, and the reflector's timestamps let the sender account for processing delay. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that later RFCs have updated.

today: RFC 5357 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5618, RFC 5938, RFC 6038, RFC 7717, RFC 7750 and RFC 8545, so read it together with those.

sections.title: Why a Two-Way Protocol
sections.content:
The IETF already had a protocol for one-way measurements, the One-way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656). OWAMP can be run in both directions to get one-way numbers each way, but it does not accommodate round-trip or two-way measurements.

The RFC says two-way measurements are common in IP networks. Synchronization between local and remote clocks is unnecessary for round-trip delay, and support at the remote end may be limited to a simple echo function. The usual tool for this is the ICMP Echo Request/Reply used by ping, and its issues are documented in Section 2.6 of RFC 2681.

TWAMP keeps OWAMP's methodology and architecture. It adds timestamps applied at the echo destination (the reflector), so processing delays can be accounted for. Because a TWAMP setup usually has only two hosts with specific roles, some protocol simplifications are possible, which the RFC calls an attractive alternative to OWAMP in some circumstances.
sections.eli5: Ping is a quick shout across the yard and listening for the echo. TWAMP is a more careful version where your friend writes down exactly when your shout arrived and when they shouted back.

sections.title: Roles and the Two Protocols
sections.content:
TWAMP is made of two inter-related protocols, as in OWAMP. TWAMP-Control is used to initiate, start and stop test sessions. TWAMP-Test is used to exchange test packets between two TWAMP entities.

The logical roles come from OWAMP with a few changes:

  • The Control-Client starts the control connection and the Server answers it.
  • The Session-Sender sends test packets.
  • The Session-Receiver of OWAMP is called the Session-Reflector. It creates and sends a measurement packet when it receives one, but unlike a Session-Receiver it does not collect any packet information.
  • There is no Fetch-Client, because the reflector collects nothing to fetch.

Several roles can live on one host. The usual two-host layout puts the Control-Client and Session-Sender on one host and the Server and Session-Reflector on the other. All multi-octet quantities are unsigned integers in network byte order, and bits marked MBZ (Must Be Zero) MUST be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.eli5: One kid runs the game and throws the ball. The other kid runs the scoreboard and catches and returns the ball. They can be two people or, with a friend's help, even more.

sections.title: The Control Connection
sections.content:
The Control-Client opens a TCP connection to the Server on well-known port 862. The Server replies with a Greeting that lists the security modes it supports. The client picks a mode, the Server accepts it and gives its start time, and the connection is ready. Connection setup, integrity protection (HMAC) and the Accept field values all follow the OWAMP rules, and the current mode values are identical to OWAMP's.

The client then requests one or more test sessions, sends a Start-Sessions message to begin them, and later a Stop-Sessions message to end them. The Control-Client MAY set a Diffserv Code Point on its control packets, and the Server SHOULD reuse the DSCP of the client's TCP SYN.

To free resources after failures, the Server MAY drop a control connection that has been silent for SERVWAIT seconds, and a Session-Reflector MAY drop a session that has been silent for REFWAIT seconds. The default for both is 900 seconds.

The Modes field and the Command Number are the two recognized extension mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Before throwing the ball, the two kids agree on the rules over a phone call. If one stops answering for a long time, the other hangs up.

sections.title: Requesting and Stopping Sessions
sections.content:
TWAMP adds one command beyond OWAMP. Request-TW-Session has Command Number 5 and replaces OWAMP's Request-Session. It uses the OWAMP format without the Schedule Slot Descriptions and with only one HMAC. The Fetch-Session command is not used at all, because everything the sender needs comes back in the reflected packets.

Several fields are fixed or reinterpreted:

  • Conf-Sender and Conf-Receiver MUST both be 0, since the reflector both receives and sends. Any non-zero value gets an Accept value of 3 (some aspect of request is not supported).
  • Number of Scheduled Slots and Number of Packets MUST be 0, and the SID in the request MUST be 0 because the Server picks it.
  • The sender uses the same UDP port to send and receive. The reflector does likewise on its Receiver Port. If the requested port is busy, the Server MAY suggest another in the Port field.
  • Timeout is how long the reflector MUST keep reflecting packets still in transit after it gets Stop-Sessions. Later packets MUST NOT be reflected.

The sender is free to choose its own send schedule. The reflector SHOULD return each packet as quickly as possible. Stop-Sessions (Command Number 3) can only come from the Control-Client and applies to all sessions started. Its Number of Sessions MUST match the sessions in progress, or the message is invalid.
sections.eli5: The thrower says, "Catch whatever I send and throw it straight back." There is no schedule for the reflector to follow, because it just returns everything it catches.

sections.title: Test Packets and Reflector Behavior
sections.content:
TWAMP-Test has two packet formats, one for the Session-Sender and a larger one for the Session-Reflector. As in OWAMP there are three modes: unauthenticated, authenticated and encrypted.

For every packet it receives, the reflector MUST do the following:

  • Record the best possible approximation of the arrival time as the Receive Timestamp.
  • Copy the sender's sequence number into Sender Sequence Number, and give the reflected packet its own independent Sequence Number starting at zero.
  • Copy the sender's timestamp and error estimate into Sender Timestamp and Sender Error Estimate.
  • Set Sender TTL from the TTL or Hop Limit of the received packet (the sender sets 255). If it cannot read the TTL it MUST set 255.
  • Send the reply as immediately as possible, with its own transmit Timestamp. The difference between Timestamp and Receive Timestamp is the time the packet spent inside the reflector.

Because the reflector's packet is larger, the sender can append Packet Padding (at least 27 octets unauthenticated, at least 56 in the other modes) so both directions have equal IP payload lengths. The minimum data segment is 41 octets in unauthenticated mode and 104 in authenticated and encrypted modes. Padding SHOULD be pseudo-random but implementations MUST offer an all-zeros option, and padding is never covered by the HMAC or encrypted.

In authenticated mode the first 16-octet block is encrypted with AES in ECB mode. In encrypted mode the first 96 octets are encrypted with AES-CBC and the HMAC covers the same range. The test keys are derived from the control keys and the session identifier.
sections.eli5: The catcher stamps the ball with the time it arrived, copies what the thrower wrote on it, adds the time it leaves, and throws it back. The thrower can then subtract to find the real travel time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TWAMP and OWAMP use the same protocol for control and test setup. The only main difference is reflector versus receiver behavior, which the RFC says introduces no known security vulnerability not already handled by OWAMP, so all of OWAMP's security considerations apply.

One addition concerns the Count field in the Server-Greeting, a 32-bit PKCS #5 iteration counter used to derive keys. An attacker could set it to the maximum and make the victim stall while generating keys. TWAMP systems SHOULD have a configuration control that limits the maximum Count, with a suggested default maximum of 32768. A client that receives a larger Count SHOULD close the control connection.
sections.eli5: Someone could ask you to do a ridiculously long math problem just to waste your time. So you set a limit on how hard a problem you will accept.

sections.title: Implementer's Guide and TWAMP Light
sections.content:
The RFC suggests, as an example and not a requirement, a controller host (Control-Client and Session-Sender) and a responder host (Server and Session-Reflector).

Appendix I, which is informative, describes an incremental path called TWAMP Light. The controller holds the Control-Client, Server and Session-Sender roles, while the responder runs only the Session-Reflector. Test sessions are set up by non-standard means and TWAMP-Control is not used. A reflector that has no session state MUST copy the received Sequence Number into the reflected packet. The non-standard control channel SHOULD offer an authenticated mode, and a reflector using authenticated or encrypted test mode needs its own key generation, which is outside the RFC's scope.

IANA also created a TWAMP-Control Command Number registry of sixteen possible values, changed by IETF Consensus. Value 6 is allocated for experimentation.
sections.eli5: If you only want the ball returned, you can skip the phone call entirely and just have a friend who returns every ball that arrives.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Reflector's own sequence number, starting at zero.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: When the reflector received the sender's packet.

fields.name: Sender Sequence Number
fields.desc: Copy of the sender packet's sequence number.

fields.name: Sender Timestamp
fields.desc: Exact copy of the sender's timestamp.

fields.name: Sender Error Estimate
fields.desc: Exact copy of the sender's error estimate.

fields.name: Sender TTL
fields.desc: TTL or Hop Limit of the received packet; the sender sets 255.
